title: Why sums look normal
objectives: Watch sums from any distribution become normal, and state the central limit theorem
Approximate the chance that a sum passes a level
Recognise when the theorem does not apply

screens.title: Average some waits
screens.prose: Waits between trades are often exponential: mostly short, now and then long. Average $n$ waits, then rescale so the mean is 0 and the sd is 1. Slide $n$.

derive.caption: Waits averaged: {{n}}. Bars: exact chances. Dashes: the normal.

screens.question: As $n$ goes from 1 to 30, what happens to the shape of the bars?

options.text: It loses its lean and hugs the dashed normal
It keeps the shape of a single wait
options.why: You watched one end of the slider. Slide to 30: the long right tail shrinks and a left tail grows.

options.text: It collapses to a spike at 0
options.why: An unscaled average would collapse onto the mean. We rescaled to sd 1, so only the shape can change.

options.text: It flattens out across the axis
options.why: Slide to 30 and read the middle bars: they rise towards 0.19, the height of the dashes.

hints.text: Compare the picture at $n = 1$ with the picture at $n = 30$.
At $n = 1$ the bars start at $-1$ and trail off to the right. At 30, compare them with the dashes.

feedback.correct: By 30 waits the bars sit close to the dashes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 30 and compare the bars with the dashes.

explain.text: One wait is lopsided: it cannot fall below its mean by more than 1 sd. Averaging 30 waits gives a nearly symmetric bell, though a slight lean to the right remains. The normal shape came from averaging, not from the waits.

screens.title: Undo the rescaling
screens.prose: Each wait has mean 1 minute and sd 1 minute. The sum $S$ of 30 independent waits has mean $30$ minutes.
screens.question: What is the sd of $S$, in minutes? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the 30 variances, then take the square root.

byKey.var: That is the variance of $S$. The sd is its square root.
byKey.one: That is the sd of one wait. Summing 30 widens it.
byKey.mean: That is the sd of the average, $1/\sqrt{30}$. The question asks about the sum.

explain.text: The sum has mean $n\mu = 30$ and sd $\sigma\sqrt n \approx 5.48$. So $Z = (S - 30)/5.48$, which is also $(\bar X - 1)/(1/\sqrt{30})$. The sum and the average make the same rescaled picture.

screens.title: Lopsided starts are slower
screens.prose: Top: averages of exponential waits, which lean right. Bottom: averages of uniform draws on 0 to 1, which are symmetric. Both are rescaled the same way.
screens.question: At $n = 3$, which average is already close to the normal?

options.text: The uniform average
The exponential average
options.why: Look at its left edge at $n = 3$: almost nothing below $-1.5$, while the normal has 0.07 there.

options.text: Both equally
options.why: Compare their tallest bars with the dashes. The uniform matches; the exponential still peaks left of 0.

options.text: Neither, since 3 draws are never enough
options.why: You applied a fixed rule of thumb. The uniform at 3 already sits within 0.01 of each dash.

hints.text: Compare each panel's bars with its dashes.
Check which panel is still lopsided.

feedback.correct: A symmetric, light-tailed start reaches the bell quickly.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the panel whose bars match the dashes.

explain.text: The uniform has no lean, so three draws already look normal. The exponential's lean fades slowly, roughly like $1/\sqrt n$. How fast the bell appears depends on how lopsided one draw is and how heavy its tails are.

screens.title: More data, same shape
screens.prose: An analyst records 1,000 single waits and says: with this much data, the central limit theorem makes the waits normal. Run the draws.

state.caption: Each trial is one wait, not an average

screens.question: After 1,000 draws, what does the histogram of single waits look like?

options.text: The exponential shape, lopsided as ever
A bell, since 1,000 is a large sample
options.why: You applied the theorem to the draws themselves. It is about sums and averages; a histogram of draws shows the draws.

options.text: Flat, since every wait becomes equally likely
options.why: More draws trace the true shape more sharply. They never flatten it.

hints.text: Press Run 1,000 and compare the bars with the dashes.
The dashes are the exponential, the shape of one wait.

feedback.correct: More draws only sharpen the picture of one wait.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 draws and look at the shape.

byKey.normal: You applied the theorem to the draws themselves. It is about sums and averages; a histogram of draws shows the draws.

explain.text: The histogram tracks the exponential dashes, not a bell. A large sample shows the true shape of one draw more clearly. Only sums or averages of many draws turn normal.

screens.title: The central limit theorem
screens.prose: You rescaled averages and watched the bell appear. Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent, identically distributed, with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$. Then $$\frac{\bar X_n - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt n} \to N(0, 1) \text{ as } n \to \infty.$$ The shape of one draw does not matter.
screens.question: Which condition can the theorem not do without?

options.text: Each draw has a finite variance
Each draw is normal
options.why: The waits were exponential and their averages still became normal.

options.text: Each draw is symmetric
options.why: The exponential is lopsided, yet its averages reached the bell. Symmetry only speeds it up.

options.text: At least 30 draws are averaged
options.why: Thirty is a rule of thumb, not a condition. The uniform looked normal at 3.

hints.text: Which assumption appears in the statement above?

feedback.correct: A finite variance is needed; the shape is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check what the statement assumes about $\sigma^2$.

explain.text: This form of the theorem assumes independent, identical draws and a finite $\sigma^2$; other forms relax the first two. Divide by $\sigma/\sqrt n$ and the limit is $N(0, 1)$ whatever the starting shape. That is why sums of many small effects look normal.

screens.title: Sum or average, same $Z$
screens.prose: Let $S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n$, so $\bar X_n = S_n / n$. Show that rescaling the sum gives the same $Z$ as rescaling the average.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $\operatorname{Var}(S_n) = n\sigma^2$, since the variances of independent draws add
$Z = \dfrac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}$, subtract the mean and divide by the sd
$= \dfrac{S_n / n - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt n} = \dfrac{\bar X_n - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt n}$, dividing top and bottom by $n$

hints.text: You need the mean and the variance of $S_n$ before you can rescale it.
Mean, variance, rescale, then divide top and bottom by $n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the mean and variance of the sum before rescaling it.

byKey.z: The rescaling uses the mean and sd of $S_n$. Find those first.
byKey.div: Dividing by $n$ turns the sum into the average. It comes once $Z$ is written for the sum.

explain.text: So the theorem can be read for sums too: $S_n \approx N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)$ for large $n$. You used exactly this in the 30-wait screen. Next we use it to put a number on a sum.

screens.title: A normal approximation to a sum
screens.prose: A desk processes 50 orders in a row. Each takes an exponential time with mean 1 minute and sd 1 minute. Use $\Phi(1.4142) = 0.9214$.
screens.question: Approximately, what is the chance the 50 orders take more than 60 minutes?

hints.text: $z = 10/7.071 = 1.4142$, and you want the upper tail.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Standardise 60 with mean 50 and sd 7.07, then take the upper tail.

byKey.phi: That is $P(S \le 60)$. You want the chance of more than 60.
byKey.sd-50: You used 50 as the sd. The variance is 50, so the sd is about 7.07.

explain.text: The normal gives 0.0786. The exact answer for a sum of 50 exponentials is 0.0844. The normal is a little low because a faint right lean survives at $n = 50$.

screens.title: When no limit is needed
screens.prose: Suppose a stock's daily returns are exactly normal, mean 0.05% and sd 1%, independent across days. Consider the sum of $n$ daily returns.
screens.question: How large must $n$ be for that sum to be normal?

options.text: Any $n$: a sum of independent normals is exactly normal
About 30, the usual rule of thumb
options.why: The rule of thumb is for lopsided starts. Normal draws are already at the limit.

options.text: It is never exactly normal, only close
options.why: For normal draws the sum is exactly normal at every $n$, even $n = 2$.

options.text: Large enough to swamp the 0.05% mean
options.why: The mean only shifts the bell. It never stops the sum being normal.

hints.text: The theorem describes where a shape ends up. Where does a normal start?

feedback.correct: Normals add to normals, with means and variances adding too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what the limit is, and where these draws start.

explain.text: A sum of $n$ independent $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ draws is exactly $N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)$. Two days give mean 0.1% and sd $\sqrt 2 \approx 1.41\%$, as drawn. The theorem matters when draws are not normal.

screens.title: Daily against monthly returns
screens.prose: A day's return is the sum of thousands of trades' price effects. In calm markets daily returns look roughly normal. In stress they show fat tails, and big days cluster together. Returns here are log returns, which add across days.

state.caption: A fat-tailed shape (solid) beside a normal with the same sd (dashed)

screens.question: Compare 20-day returns with daily returns. Which is right?

options.text: 20-day returns look closer to normal, though clustering slows the approach
Daily returns must be exactly normal, since each sums thousands of trades
options.why: Those trades are not independent, and some effects are huge. The theorem's conditions fail inside a day.

options.text: 20-day returns are less normal, since they span more days
options.why: A 20-day return is a sum of 20 daily ones. Summing pulls the shape towards the bell.

options.text: With 1,000 daily returns, the theorem makes the daily returns normal
options.why: That is the trap again: more observations sharpen the shape of one day. They do not change it.

hints.text: A 20-day return is a sum. What does the theorem say about sums?
Then ask whether the days are truly independent.

feedback.correct: Sums of days move towards normal, slowed by dependence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat the 20-day return as a sum of 20 daily returns.

explain.text: Summing 20 days thins the tails, so monthly returns look more normal than daily ones. Volatility clusters, so the days are not independent, and the approach is slower than for independent days. Fat tails with infinite variance would block it entirely.

screens.title: A book of small bets
screens.prose: A book holds 400 independent positions. Each has expected P&L £50 and sd £1,000 over the month. Use $\Phi(-1) = 0.1587$.

params.xLabel: Book P&L over the month (£ thousands)

screens.question: Approximately, what is the chance the book loses money over the month?

hints.text: Mean £20,000 and sd £20,000: zero is 1 sd below the mean.

feedback.correct: Zero sits 1 sd below the mean: $\Phi(-1) = 0.1587$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the book's mean and sd, then standardise 0.

byKey.sd-sum: That treats the book as centred on zero. Its mean is $400 \times 50 = 20{,}000$ pounds.
byKey.no-scale: You kept the sd of one position, £1,000, for the whole book. Variances add, so the sd grows to £20,000.
byKey.sd-n: You scaled the sd by 400, or used one position alone. The book's sd is $1000\sqrt{400} = 20{,}000$ pounds.

explain.text: Means add to £20,000; variances add to $400 \times 1000^2$, so the sd is £20,000. The chance of a losing month is $\Phi(-1) \approx 0.16$. Independence is doing the work: positively correlated positions would widen the bell.

ideas: Rescaled sums and averages of independent, identically distributed draws with finite variance approach $N(0, 1)$, whatever one draw looks like.
For large $n$, $S_n \approx N(n\mu, n\sigma^2)$ and $\bar X_n \approx N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$.
Lopsided draws need larger $n$; normal draws need none; infinite variance or strong dependence can block the limit.

formula.name: Central limit theorem
formula.note: Independent, identically distributed draws with finite variance.

summary.trap: The theorem is about sums and averages. A big sample of single draws still shows the shape of one draw.

quiz.prose: Daily returns are independent with mean 0.04% and sd 1.2%.
quiz.question: By the central limit theorem, the average over 144 days is approximately normal with what sd? Give a percentage.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the daily sd by $\sqrt{144}$.

byKey.over-n: You divided by 144. The sd of an average shrinks with $\sqrt n$.
byKey.sum: That is the sd of the sum, $1.2\% \times 12$. The question asks about the average.

explain.text: $\bar X \approx N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$, so its sd is $1.2\% / 12 = 0.1\%$.

quiz.prose: Each option describes $n$ draws that are averaged.
quiz.question: For which draws can the central limit theorem not promise a normal average?

options.text: Draws with no finite variance, such as a Cauchy
Coin tosses scored 0 or 1
options.why: A 0 or 1 draw has variance $\tfrac14$. Its averages do become normal.

options.text: Exponential waits
options.why: Lopsided, but with variance 1. You watched their averages become normal.

options.text: Rolls of a fair die
options.why: A die has variance $\tfrac{35}{12}$, finite. Its averages become normal.

feedback.correct: Without a finite variance the theorem does not apply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the draw whose variance is not finite.

explain.text: The theorem divides by $\sigma/\sqrt n$, so it needs a finite $\sigma$. The average of $n$ Cauchy draws is again Cauchy, however large $n$ is.

quiz.prose: You roll 100 fair dice. One die has mean 3.5 and variance $\tfrac{35}{12}$. Use $\Phi(1.17) = 0.879$.
quiz.question: Approximately, what is the chance the total exceeds 370?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Standardise 370 with the sum's mean and sd.

byKey.lower: That is the chance the total is at most 370. Take the upper tail.
byKey.var-sd: Use the sd, $\sqrt{291.7} \approx 17.08$, not the variance.

explain.text: The total has mean $350$ and sd $\sqrt{291.7} \approx 17.08$. So $z \approx 1.17$ and the chance is about $0.121$.

quiz.prose: Measurement errors in a lab are often close to normal.
quiz.question: Which explanation fits the central limit theorem?

options.text: Each error is the sum of many small independent effects
Nature prefers the normal for every single quantity
options.why: Many single quantities are lopsided, like waits. Sums of many effects are what turn normal.

options.text: The lab takes many measurements
options.why: Many measurements show the shape of one error more sharply; they do not create it.

feedback.correct: Many small independent nudges add up to a bell.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the theorem says gets added.

explain.text: The theorem is about sums. An error built from many small independent nudges is such a sum, so it comes out close to normal.
